newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Smaller Asia markets seen dodging Dow jitters in week ahead.
newsitem.headline: Smaller Asia markets seen dodging Dow jitters in week ahead.

text.p: Major Asian stock markets such as Hong Kong, Tokyo and Sydney could catch a case of the jitters from a struggling Wall Street in the week ahead, but traders said smaller bourses could remain immune.
"Indonesia is looking good," said a regional trader. "Malaysia looks as though it's got a bit more fire there as well."
But markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sydney and Wellington are expected to follow the Dow Jones index, which sank 59 points to 6696.48 on Friday.

Volatility on Wall Street is expected to push Hong Kong stocks to a test of the 13,000 level. The blue-chip Hang Seng Index closed on Friday at 13,379.55, down 476.85 points or 3.44 percent on the week.
It was the market's worst weekly decline in 10 months.
In Tokyo, brokers said a lack of domestic news could also direct attention to New York.
In the interim, futures-linked trade will drive the market, which remains weighed down by uncertainty over the economy and the health of the financial sector.
Sydney and Wellington were also expected to keep a close eye on Wall Street, which is seen consolidating at current levels following its third consecutive decline on Friday.
The U.S. market is suffering from mounting interest rate pressure and increasing concern about its near-term outlook.
Among the other small Asian markets, opinion remained divided over the fate of laggards Thailand and Korea, with many foreign investors hoping for recovery sometime this year.
Traders are also optimistic that the Philippines will rise further on news of a possible sovereign debt rating upgrade from Moody's Investors Service Inc.
HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks are expected to fall further in the week ahead, possibly testing 13,000 to 13,200 points as investors watch volatility on Wall Street, brokers said.
The Hang Seng tumbled 230.78 points, or 1.70 percent, on Friday to 13,379.55.

"Investors have seen the market come down for a week and they are staying on the sidelines. I expect there still to be some selling pressure but there should be some support at 13,000 points," said Peter So of Schroder Securities.
"If they see momentum return then they will come back."
Futures trading was also expected to dominate activity ahead of Thursday's expiration of the January future.
TOKYO - Tokyo stocks are expected to be volatile, driven by futures-linked trade and racked by persistent uncertainty over the economy and the health of the financial sector.
The benchmark Nikkei average rebounded sharply on January 22 but was unable to hold above the 18,000 threshold for long.
"Selling pressure is heavy near that level...," an analyst at Dai-ichi Securities said. "On the other hand, thanks to the rebound,chances of a fall below 17,000 are looking less likely."
Brokers said that the lack of domestic direction was turning attention to the Dow industrials. The sagging of the yen to the 119 level against the dollar was also a concern.
SYDNEY - Australian shares were seen shaky in the near term as nervous local investors watched Wall Street.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,423, down 12.5 points over the week despite reaching record highs and closes of 2,456.7 and 2,444.2 respectively on January 20.
Profit-taking cropped the benchmark from its highs early in the week while Friday's trade ahead of a local holiday weekend was predictably dominated by sellers cutting positions.
JAKARTA - Share prices are expected to rise in the coming week although some market players think some counters have peaked, brokers said.
Expectations of higher 1996 earnings in some sectors could boost sentiment, brokers said. One analyst said Bank Negara Indonesia was likely to remain a major focus of attention.
Jakarta's Composite Index ended the week 14.94 points or 2.25 percent higher at 678.91 points on Friday.
MANILA - The main Manila index may take another run at an all-time high of 3,375 in the coming week, boosted by strong earnings and news of a possible sovereign debt rating upgrade.
The index ended 38.22 points or 1.16 percent stronger on the week at 3,332.53 following a 4.15-point rise on Friday.
The index broke out of a strong 3,300 resistance level last week and is seen gaining steadily on good corporate results.

KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian shares are expected to rise further in the coming week after closing 2.26 points higher on Friday at 1,244.13 thanks to institutional fund buying and data showing a shrinking trade deficit, brokers said.
Kuala Lumpur's Composite Index climbed 2.26 points to 1244.13 on Friday, ending the week 19.58 points or 1.59 percent stronger against a close of 1224.55 on January 17.
SEOUL - The negative impact of Hanbo Steel's default on over five billion won worth of debt last Thursday will continue to weaken banking shares and depress the market, brokers said.

"The market next week really depends on how the government resolves the Hanbo issue," said Lee Duck-jae, a broker at Dongwon Securities. On Friday, the composite index closed at 679.56, 21.62 points or 3.08 percent lower on the week.
Foreign traders in Hong Kong said opinion remains divided on South Korea, which is depressed by poor economic fundamentals.
BANGKOK - The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index is expected to fall slightly next week as investors await 1996 earnings results and monthly economic data, brokers said.
The SET index closed 16.01 points weaker at 848.56 on Friday, up 16.01 points or 1.92 percent on the week.
Regional traders said they were expecting further short-term weakness in the coming week following last week's spurt.
